item.title: Can a Temporary Break From Drinking Make Moderation Easier?
item.description:
Alcoholism

Can a Temporary Break From Drinking Make Moderation Easier?

A brief period without alcohol may improve one's success with moderation.

Posted July 13, 2026

Key points
  • Taking a break from drinking can help to clarify and change your relationship with alcohol.
  • A sober month or more can improve your chances of moderating afterward.
  • Temporary abstinence is an informative and empowering strategy, not an endpoint.
  • Professional guidance and support can amplify and extend the clinical benefits of sobriety sampling.

Rethinking the Question of Abstinence

Most people who want to cut back on drinking assume the best strategy is to somehow force themselves to simply drink less. Surprisingly, research suggests that taking a temporary break from alcohol may actually improve the chances of long-term moderation. Rather than reflecting an all-or-nothing philosophy, a planned period of temporary abstinence can help reset habits, build confidence, and make later moderation more achievable.

Self-guided breaks from drinking can be beneficial. Professionally guided breaks supplemented by real-time support from an addiction psychologist or other specialist practitioner can further amplify and extend those benefits.

Hit the Reset Button

Taking alcohol off the table for several weeks or longer interrupts automatic drinking routines. Without the daily negotiation over whether to have “just one,” people can step back and observe why, when, and how they drink. Studies of initiatives such as “Dry January” suggest that many participants continue drinking less long after the challenge ends.

Rewiring the Brain

A temporary break also weakens learned associations between alcohol and everyday situations. Stress, celebrations, restaurants, and weekends often become automatic cues to drink. Time away from alcohol helps loosen those conditioned links and encourages healthier ways of relaxing, socializing, and coping with emotions.

Building Confidence

Successfully completing a month without alcohol strengthens “self-efficacy,” the belief that you can control your drinking rather than being controlled by it. That confidence often carries forward when alcohol is reintroduced, making moderation feel like a deliberate choice instead of a wrestling match.

A Fresh Perspective

Stepping away from alcohol also provides valuable insight. Many people discover they were drinking on “autopilot,” more from habit, boredom, stress, or social expectation than genuine enjoyment. This new awareness makes it easier to establish realistic, sustainable drinking goals.

The Physical Payoff

Even a short alcohol-free period can improve sleep, energy, concentration, mood, blood pressure, and weight. Experiencing these benefits firsthand often becomes a powerful incentive to maintain healthier drinking habits.

Who Is This Approach For?

This strategy is most appropriate for people with mild to moderate alcohol problems whose goal is moderation. It is not appropriate for everyone. Individuals with severe alcohol use disorder or a history of significant withdrawal symptoms should seek professional medical guidance before attempting abstinence because unmanaged alcohol withdrawal can pose serious health dangers.

The Bottom Line

A temporary break from alcohol is more than an exercise in willpower. It offers an opportunity to reset habits, gain perspective, improve health, and strengthen confidence. Ongoing support and guidance from a knowledgeable clinician can help to realize and optimize these benefits. For many people hoping to become moderate drinkers, the shortest path to drinking less may begin, somewhat paradoxically, with a guided attempt at not drinking at all.

item.title: To Risk, or Not to Risk?
item.description:
Self-Help

To Risk, or Not to Risk?

If you want to flourish, you have to embrace both excitement and fear.

Posted July 13, 2026

Key points
  • Just when you think everything's perfect, your intuition may indicate otherwise.
  • Expect anxiety and uncertainty when you take risks.
  • Making change doesn't come without loss, but it certainly is worthwhile.

Everybody’s afraid of change.

Admit it: you are. I’ll admit it: I am. But there are people who manage to get past their fear of change and embrace it. (I find those people fascinating.) Others resist until the very last minute.

Which one describes you?

How many of you are living your lives knowing you’re reasonably happy, or living a routine you’re comfortable with, and sticking to safety and maintenance, even though a part of you might know you need—or want—more? Are there relationships or activities that you have thought about pursuing but never tried? Have you postponed travel that had the potential to be exciting, but you saw only obstacles? Did you think about moving but instead decided to stay put in a city or neighborhood that’s known and comfortable?

Source: The 5th/Unsplash

As some of us settle into middle age and beyond, it’s easy to enjoy and never question the safety and security we experience in our routines, our homes, our communities. And that’s a valid and sometimes excellent choice to make. We’ve worked hard all these years—at our careers, in our relationships, with our families—so that we can belong, fit in, and achieve success.

But it’s also helpful to occasionally step back from our achievements and our lifestyles and ask if it’s what we really want. Our unconscious minds have a great deal of power, and when the unconscious speaks, it often does so through intuition—and no matter what choice you ultimately make, intuition is generally your friend.

Taking risks is one of the hardest things in life: it’s destabilizing, guarantees no specific outcome, and triggers fear of the unknown. But it’s also a double-edged sword: in order to live fully, you need to take on some challenges, including (or especially) those you find scary.

Which isn’t to say that every risk should be taken on, every danger accepted. How many people do you know who go out of their way to take on risks: rock climbers, parachute jumpers, adrenaline junkies? Getting a thrill can also be an excuse for unsafe sexual practices or drug experimentation, which are clearly unhealthy responses to the risk/routine dichotomy.

Still, many of us have dreams we watch others claim while we stay at home and observe from the sidelines. And often people who take risks have a certain kind of energy, excitement, and confidence; it’s a truism that at the end of life, most people regret not having experienced something rather than regretting the things they tried.

Source: Faruk Tokluoglu/Unsplash

I’ve been thinking about this a lot lately. A few years ago, visiting the Hudson River Valley for a simple getaway, I was taken aback by my reaction to this idyllic place. My partner and I had lived on Cape Cod for over 30 years, loving our house and our neighborhood and believing it was where we’d end our days. So I was surprised at the thought of moving anywhere else... But there was some sort of magical pull that I kept going back to again and again. Why not do it now? The thought was both exciting... and completely petrifying.

After that initial shock, though, everything lined up quickly: we found a house in a fabulous area, listed ours, and a few months later, the truck was packed up, and we were on our way to a new life. And in the year since then, we’ve been constantly reviewing what led us to make this change, and the word that best sums it up is expansive: we expanded our ideas of what we wanted, of where we belonged, even of who we were.

All this led me to think about taking risks versus maintaining a routine. Many people are perfectly happy in their lives and don’t need to consider a change; I was one of them. I was initially shocked at the thought of even considering making such a fundamental change, but that shock wasn’t enough to scare me away from considering other possibilities.

And that’s where there’s a tremendous gift waiting: we all have the opportunity to make changes if we choose to do so. The change might not be as radical as relocation to another part of the country, but it may still be scary. Exploring options, even if only in your mind, can keep you young and vibrant and open.

Is something pulling you as the Hudson River Valley was pulling me? Continuing your education? Becoming a foster parent? Traveling abroad? Are you brave enough to give the possibility of change a place in your heart?

Source: Ryan Porter/Unsplash

Considering change involves making a choice, and sometimes the choice is not to go after the change. A friend of mine on the Cape, a writer searching for more isolation, decided a few years ago to move to a remote town in Nova Scotia. A number of red flags were raised for her in the process, and she ultimately decided to stay where she was—but to remodel her cottage instead. Change doesn’t have to be drastic to be invigorating and fulfilling!

It’s all making me ask questions. What is change, and why do we resist allowing ourselves to pursue it? Think about who you are: Are you drawn to the excitement of making changes, or do you hold tightly to past choices you’ve made?

The point is that you can have choices now, and you can make changes now. You have it in you. You can live the excitement of life by incorporating novelty, taking risks, and simply listening to yourself and imagining what you want for this season of your life.

Be bold. Try new things. Don’t postpone your dreams until there’s a “better” time for them: that time is now.

Source: Suzanne D. Williams/Unsplash
